original_question: For the hard-core lattice gas on general graphs, what happens at non-small fugacity w: when does one have uniqueness versus nonuniqueness of infinite-volume Gibbs measures as a function of w, what are the large-w Gibbs measures, and are the phase transitions first-order or second-order?
target_in_paper: The draft is aiming at the unnumbered open-problem cluster in the hard-core lattice-gas part of the survey: characterize, for an infinite graph, the equilibrium phase diagram in the fugacity w, i.e. uniqueness versus nonuniqueness of infinite-volume Gibbs measures, the nature of the large-fugacity phases, and the order of the transition. In this paper these questions are discussed in Section 2 as part of the equilibrium-properties agenda for the hard-core lattice gas, not as a numbered conjecture.
correct_elements: Your draft captures the right topic and the right three subquestions from the paper’s hard-core-lattice-gas equilibrium discussion: (i) uniqueness versus nonuniqueness of infinite-volume Gibbs measures, (ii) description of the large-fugacity phases/Gibbs measures, and (iii) whether the transition is first-order or second-order. It also correctly uses the fugacity parameter w and stays on the equilibrium side of the paper rather than drifting into partition-function zeros or Monte Carlo dynamics.
missing_details: The graph should be specified as infinite; otherwise 'infinite-volume Gibbs measure' is undefined.
The hard-core model should be defined explicitly: configurations are independent sets (or 0/1 occupations with no adjacent occupied vertices), weighted by w^{|I|} in finite volume.
The fugacity should be stated as a positive real parameter w > 0.
It should be clear that the question concerns DLR/infinite-volume Gibbs measures, not merely finite-volume measures.
The phrase 'non-small fugacity' is vague; the paper’s issue is to determine the phase diagram as a function of w, especially the large-w regime and possible critical value(s).
If one keeps the scope broad, one should say 'for a countably infinite locally finite (typically bounded-degree) graph G'; otherwise the graph-theoretic setting is underspecified.
The phrase 'large-w Gibbs measures' should be sharpened to 'the extremal infinite-volume Gibbs measures that arise for sufficiently large w'.
The transition whose order is being asked about should be identified as the order-disorder phase transition in the fugacity parameter w.

The draft says 'general graphs', but the paper’s nearby discussion is a survey-style equilibrium question and is most naturally read in the standard hard-core setting on infinite graphs/lattices; if one wants to stay closest to the paper, one should avoid suggesting a broader classification than the survey itself explicitly formulates.
refined_question: For the hard-core lattice gas on an infinite locally finite graph G, with finite-volume weights proportional to w^{|I|} on independent sets I and fugacity w > 0, determine the equilibrium phase diagram as a function of w: for which w is the infinite-volume Gibbs measure unique, for which w is it nonunique, what are the extremal Gibbs measures that occur for sufficiently large w, and when a transition occurs, is the resulting order-disorder transition first-order or second-order?
justification: The paper is a survey of unnumbered open problems rather than a theorem/conjecture paper with a single formal statement. In its hard-core-lattice-gas equilibrium discussion, Sokal explicitly frames the unresolved issues in exactly the direction your draft points: understanding uniqueness/nonuniqueness of infinite-volume Gibbs measures, identifying the ordered phases at large fugacity, and determining the nature of the phase transition. Your draft is therefore substantively on target, but it is not yet fully stand-alone because it leaves implicit the model definition, the infinite-graph setting, the positivity and role of the fugacity w, and the fact that the relevant objects are infinite-volume DLR Gibbs measures. The refined version above keeps the scope narrow and faithful to the paper’s intent without broadening to neighboring problems such as partition-function zeros or mixing times.
